clue.text: Essex resort equal to Holyhead ?

parts.note: Holyhead, the Welsh port, joins a word to an extremity of the body or land; the Essex seaside town wanted is named on the same pattern, a compass point joined to an extremity

explanation.surface: A geography question comparing an English seaside town with a Welsh ferry port.
explanation.walkthrough: Holyhead is a port on Anglesey; the clue asks for the Essex resort whose name is built the same way, a point of the compass plus 'end' in place of 'head'.
explanation.definitionFit: Southend-on-Sea is the best-known seaside town in the county of Essex, east of London.

clue.text: Top dressing?

parts.note: top dressing in gardening is fertiliser spread on the soil, but here it is a garment worn over the top of other clothes

explanation.definitionFit: An overall is a loose coat or one-piece garment worn on top of ordinary clothes to protect them.

clue.text: Easily managed to get pamphlet on island rising

parts.note: a tract is a short pamphlet, often religious or political

indicators.note: rising in a down clue means the island's name is read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: Elba is the Mediterranean island where Napoleon was exiled

explanation.surface: Getting a leaflet on a revolting island would be easy to arrange.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts the second piece below the first; 'rising' turns the island upwards, giving the letters A-B-L-E. 'to get' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Tractable means docile and easy to control or handle, as of a person or a material.

clue.text: Supporters of the pre Raphaelites, for example?

definitions.text: Supporters of the pre Raphaelites, for example?

parts.words: Supporters of the pre Raphaelites, for example?
parts.note: supporters suggests admirers or patrons of the Victorian painting group, but means the stands that hold up any painter's canvas

explanation.definitionFit: An easel is a wooden frame that holds a painter's canvas upright while they work.

clue.text: Looking hellishly abashed ?

parts.note: Dis is the Roman god of the underworld and also the name of his infernal city, so hell
countenanced, having a countenance or face, is a way of describing how someone looks

explanation.surface: Someone appearing terribly embarrassed.
explanation.walkthrough: Dis, Roman lord of the dead, stands for hell. The pieces are joined in the opposite order to the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Discountenanced means put out of face, disconcerted and ashamed.

clue.text: Tradesman of coarser speech ?

indicators.note: speech means the word is to be taken as it sounds when spoken, not as written

parts.note: coarser means grosser, cruder or more vulgar

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper with a rough, vulgar way of talking.
explanation.definitionFit: A grocer is a shopkeeper selling food and household goods, one kind of tradesman.

clue.text: German leader gets let down — looked angry

indicators.note: leader means only the first letter of German is used

parts.note: to let down something is to lower it

explanation.surface: A German politician is disappointed and scowls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'let down' looks like disappointed, but it means lowered, as a bucket on a rope.
explanation.definitionFit: To glower is to stare with sullen anger, so glowered is looked angry.

clue.text: Fancy him entering race by mistake !

indicators.note: entering means the word him goes inside the jumbled letters
by mistake suggests the letters of race are put in the wrong order

explanation.surface: Imagine him wandering into a race in error!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' looks like an exclamation or a verb but is the noun, a flight of imagination. 'by mistake' jumbles the race letters as C-ERA, and 'entering' slips the pronoun in after the C.
explanation.definitionFit: A chimera is a wild fancy or illusion, from the fire-breathing monster of Greek myth.

clue.text: Little man is breaking rest of records

parts.note: Reg is the short form of Reginald, a man's name made little

indicators.note: breaking means the letters of rest are broken up and reset

explanation.surface: A small man interrupts the others' records.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaking' jumbles the word for rest into T-E-R-S, placed last; 'of' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Registers are official written lists or logs, so records.

clue.text: Virile type's view of poetess

explanation.surface: A macho man's opinion of a woman poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'view of' joins the two senses. Felicia Hemans was an English poet of the early 1800s, author of 'Casabianca' ('The boy stood on the burning deck').
explanation.definitionFit: A muscular macho man is a he-man, so 'virile type's' is he-man's; Felicia Hemans was a Romantic-era woman poet.

clue.text: Put wine in mixed gins — outrageous !

indicators.note: in tells us the wine is to be placed within the jumbled letters of gins
mixed means the letters of gins are stirred into a new order

parts.note: hock is a white wine from Germany's Rhine region

explanation.surface: Pouring wine into a cocktail of gins is scandalous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixed' jumbles the gins letters into S-ING, and 'in' sets the wine after the S. 'Put' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Something shocking scandalises people; it is outrageous.

clue.text: Cooked meat roll at the Tower

indicators.note: cooked suggests the letters of meat roll are fiddled or doctored into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A meat roll cooked at the Tower of London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooked' rearranges MEAT ROLL; 'at the' links to the definition. The surface points to the Tower of London, but the definition is a kind of tower.
explanation.definitionFit: A Martello is a small round coastal fort built in Britain against Napoleonic invasion, always called a tower.

clue.text: Many in river steamer display intemperance

indicators.note: in tells us one piece goes inside the name of the river

parts.note: the Exe is a river in Devon, south-west England
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, so many
SS stands for steamship, a steamer

explanation.surface: Lots of people on a river steamer behave without restraint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Many' as the Roman numeral for a hundred is a crossword convention; 'display' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Intemperance is going beyond due limits, overindulgence, which is excess.

clue.text: Suit the strikers!

explanation.surface: An exclamation that the people on strike should get what fits them.
explanation.definitionFit: Clubs is one of the four card suits; clubs are also cudgels, things to strike with.

clue.text: Funny type of burglar ?

parts.note: funny suggests a comic, one who makes cracks or jokes; the burglar who cracks safes is meant

explanation.definitionFit: A cracksman is an old word for a safebreaker, who cracks open safes.

clue.text: Pledge oneself to appropriate less ?

explanation.surface: Promising to take less money for oneself.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense reads the word as UNDER-TAKE: to take under the amount, so to appropriate less.
explanation.definitionFit: To undertake is to commit or bind oneself to a task; read in two parts it means taking too little.

clue.text: Light music ?

parts.note: light music normally means easy-listening, but here it is a song named after a lamp or flame one carries, burning for a lost love

explanation.definitionFit: A torch song is a sentimental ballad of unrequited love, for someone who 'carries a torch'.

clue.text: It's a gamble, in a way, about rent

indicators.note: about means the way is wrapped around the word for rent

parts.note: a route is a way from one place to another
to let is to rent out a property

explanation.surface: Gambling on property, in a manner, with the rent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' links the definition to the wordplay; 'a way' reads as 'in a manner' in the surface but is a road.
explanation.definitionFit: Roulette is the casino game of betting on where a ball lands on a spinning wheel.

clue.text: Tales one fabricated about quiet animals

indicators.note: about means the made-up letters surround the quiet sign
fabricated means the letters of tales one are made up into a new arrangement

parts.note: p, piano, is the musical direction for quiet

explanation.surface: Made-up stories about animals that keep quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fabricated' rearranges TALES ONE and 'about' wraps those letters round P.
explanation.definitionFit: Antelopes are swift, horned grazing mammals of Africa and Asia, a group of animals.

clue.text: Time 'to get the thing repaired

indicators.note: repaired, mended, suggests the letters are put back together in a new order

explanation.surface: Now is the moment to have the item fixed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'repaired' rearranges TO and THING; 'get the' links.
explanation.definitionFit: Tonight is this evening, a point or period in time.

clue.text: A stupid railwayman's effrontery ?

parts.note: BR is British Rail, the old national railway, so one of its men is BR's
an ass is a stupid person, so 'a stupid' one is an ass

explanation.surface: A foolish railway worker showing nerve.
explanation.walkthrough: BR was British Rail, the UK's state railway from 1948 to the 1990s.
explanation.definitionFit: Brass is informal British for nerve or cheek, as in 'brass neck', so effrontery.

clue.text: Someone trying a little needlework ?

explanation.surface: A person having a go at a bit of sewing.
explanation.definitionFit: A sampler is one who tastes a small portion; it is also embroidery showing a range of stitches.

clue.text: Capital saying in time of conflict

parts.note: war is a period of armed conflict
a saw is an old saying or proverb

explanation.surface: A city's motto from wartime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' only links; 'saying' looks like a verb in the surface but is the noun, an old proverb.
explanation.definitionFit: Warsaw is the capital city of Poland.

clue.text: Give name to backward boy in Westmorland

parts.note: Ken is a man's name

indicators.note: backward means the word for boy is read from end to start

parts.note: a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: Christening a slow-witted boy in the north of England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Give ... to' links the two pieces; DAL is LAD read backwards. Westmorland was a county in north-west England, now part of Cumbria.
explanation.definitionFit: Kendal is the market town that was the county town of Westmorland, so a place found there.

clue.text: Four articles to be written about Middlesex opener — curse !

indicators.note: written about means the articles are set down around the extra letter

parts.note: the four articles are an, a, the and a, the indefinite and definite articles of English

indicators.note: opener means just the first letter of Middlesex is taken

explanation.surface: A cricketing scribe writes four pieces about a Middlesex opening batsman, then swears.
explanation.walkthrough: AN, A, THE and A are written around M, the first letter of Middlesex, after THE. Middlesex is an English county cricket side, which the surface leans on.
explanation.definitionFit: An anathema is a formal ecclesiastical ban, a solemn curse, and by extension anything cursed.

clue.text: Attractive conjuring act without a net

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside means the conjuring word goes around the net

parts.note: conjuring is the performing of magic, so the act is magic

explanation.surface: A conjuror's performance appeals all the more because there is no safety net.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' here means outside, not lacking. The surface reads it as 'with no net', as for a daring circus act.
explanation.definitionFit: Magnetic means drawing things towards it, so of a person charmingly attractive.

clue.text: Mars-of course associated with war

explanation.surface: The god Mars is naturally linked with warfare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mars' looks like the Roman war god, but it is the verb 'mars', meaning damages. The second sense is the phrase 'the spoils of war'.
explanation.definitionFit: To mar something is to ruin it; and booty taken from the defeated is the plunder of war.

clue.text: Landor's first love

parts.note: the poet Walter Savage Landor wrote 'I strove with none, for none was worth my strife; ___ I loved, and next to ___, Art', so the first thing he loved

explanation.surface: A question about the first sweetheart of a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a woman Landor courted; the clue points to his best-known lines, where the outdoor world comes first and art second.
explanation.definitionFit: In Landor's quatrain 'Dying Speech of an Old Philosopher' the natural world is the first thing loved, before art.

clue.text: Titled women do business of course

parts.note: taken as written
wagers, bets, are the business done at a racecourse

explanation.surface: Aristocratic ladies carry on their affairs as a matter of course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' looks like 'naturally', but means at the racecourse, where the business is betting.
explanation.definitionFit: A dowager is a widow holding a title from her late husband, as in a dowager duchess.
